roles.name: DWP appointee
roles.summary: The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) may appoint a person over 18, or an organisation, to claim and receive social security benefits for a claimant who is 'unable for the time being to act'. DWP decides, on a written application. The appointment covers only benefits: it gives no wider power over the claimant's money.

assigned.event: Secretary of State (DWP) appoints on written application, after DWP checks that the claimant is unable to act and the applicant is suitable (form BF56, confirmed by BF57)

starts.event: On formal appointment (BF57 issued); not before

ends.event: Secretary of State revokes the appointment (e.g. appointee not acting properly, or claimant can manage own benefits)
Appointee resigns with one month's written notice

DWP is notified that a Court of Protection deputy (or Scottish guardian/judicial factor) with power over benefits exists; for UC, PIP, new-style JSA/ESA, also a registered attorney with a general or benefits power
Claimant dies. The regulations do not expressly say so: reg 33/57 cover a living person 'unable to act', and after death a separate appointment under reg 30 is needed to proceed with a claim

notes.text: Precedence: under the 1987 Regulations (legacy benefits, State Pension, AA, DLA) DWP cannot appoint if a Court of Protection deputy or Scottish guardian/judicial factor has power over benefits, and an existing appointment ends when DWP learns of one. Reg 33 does not list attorneys. Reg 57 of the 2013 Regulations (UC, PIP, new-style JSA and ESA) also excludes appointment where an attorney with a general or benefits power exists.

Extent: the 1987 and 2013 Regulations cover Great Britain. Northern Ireland benefits (Department for Communities) and devolved Scottish benefits (Social Security Scotland) have their own appointee schemes. DWP will accept those appointments as proof of authority.

After death: DWP may appoint anyone it thinks fit to proceed with a claim, and may pay arrears to personal representatives, legatees, next of kin or creditors. A written application is normally needed within 12 months of the death.
Only one appointee can act for a claimant, and the appointee takes on the claimant's duty to report changes.

transitions.event: Written application to DWP; DWP visits claimant and interviews applicant
conditions: Claimant is unable for the time being to act
No deputy (and, under reg 57, no attorney) with benefits power

transitions.event: Appointee resigns; effective after one month's written notice
DWP notified that a deputy (or, for reg 57 benefits, an attorney) with benefits power is in place
Claimant dies; any further action on the claim needs a reg 30 appointment or a personal representative
conditions: No provision expressly ends the appointment on death; inferred from scope

roles.name: Appointee for armed forces compensation / war pension
localNames: person appointed to act for M (AFCS art 71)
administration of pension by the Secretary of State (SPO art 49)
roles.summary: Armed forces compensation has its own appointment power, separate from DWP. Under the Armed Forces Compensation Scheme the Secretary of State (Defence) may appoint someone to act for a person who is incapable of managing their affairs 'by reason of mental infirmity', if no one else has legal authority. For older war pensions the Secretary of State can administer the pension directly.

assigned.event: Secretary of State appoints in writing a person (18+ if an individual). The Secretary of State must consider the person incapable of managing their affairs by reason of mental infirmity, and no one else may have legal authority to act

ends.event: Secretary of State revokes (and may appoint another)
Appointee resigns with one month's written notice
Death of the beneficiary (not stated expressly in art 71)

notes.text: Art 71 applies only where 'no person has legal authority to act on M's behalf', so an attorney or deputy takes precedence. The Secretary of State may require an undertaking on how the money will be used. The Order extends to the whole UK.

War Pensions (Service Pensions Order 2006): the Secretary of State may administer a pension where the beneficiary is, in the Secretary of State's opinion, incapable of managing their affairs by reason of mental infirmity, and apply it for their benefit. This is administration by the department, not an appointee.

transitions.event: Secretary of State appoints in writing
conditions: M incapable of managing own affairs by reason of mental infirmity
No person has legal authority to act for M

transitions.event: Appointee resigns on one month's written notice

roles.name: Personal representative dealing with HMRC for a deceased person
roles.summary: HMRC deals with the executor or administrator. By statute they are liable for income tax owed by the deceased, and for inheritance tax on the free estate, and they must file returns for both the deceased's final period and the estate's administration period. Tax law does not create a separate appointment: the role follows the person's status as personal representative under succession law.

assigned.event: Person becomes executor (named in will) or administrator (grant of letters of administration) under the law of the relevant UK jurisdiction

starts.event: From death (executor) or grant (administrator), as succession law provides; HMRC may issue a return for the deceased's pre-death income

ends.event: Estate tax affairs settled after the administration period. HMRC cannot assess PRs for the deceased's pre-death income or gains more than 4 years after the end of the tax year of death

notes.text: Income tax: the executor or administrator is liable for tax chargeable on the deceased and may pay it from the estate.
Inheritance tax: personal representatives are liable for tax on property not in a settlement, and must deliver an account.

Estate income during administration is taxed on the PRs. An estate must register with HMRC only above thresholds: estate over £2.5 million, assets sold over £500,000 in a tax year, or income tax plus CGT over £10,000. Otherwise informal arrangements apply. From 6 April 2024, estates with income up to £500 pay no income tax on it.

Tax on a living person who lacks capacity: no current TMA provision appoints a tax representative (TMA 1970 s 72, on trustees and guardians of incapacitated persons, is repealed). HMRC relies on general authority such as an attorney or deputy. Not modelled here.

states.label: Executor named in will / person entitled to grant, not yet dealing with HMRC
Dealing with HMRC as personal representative
Tax affairs of deceased and estate concluded

transitions.event: Death of a testator naming an executor, or a grant of administration
HMRC notified of death (e.g. Tell Us Once); returns issued or estate registered
Liabilities settled; assessment window for pre-death income is 4 years after the end of the tax year of death

roles.name: Applicant for a deceased patient's health records
localNames: person who may have a claim arising out of the patient's death
roles.summary: Data protection law covers only living people, so a deceased patient's records are reached through separate statutes. In England, Wales and Scotland the Access to Health Records Act 1990 lets the personal representative, and anyone who may have a claim arising from the death, apply to the record holder. Northern Ireland has a parallel Order from 1993.

assigned.event: By statute on death: the patient's personal representative, or any person who may have a claim arising out of the death. No appointment is made

starts.event: On the patient's death, by application to the holder of the record

ends.event: No statutory end date. The right lasts while the person remains personal representative or has a possible claim arising from the death

notes.text: Extent: the 1990 Act extends to England, Wales and Scotland, not Northern Ireland. The Access to Health Records (Northern Ireland) Order 1993 art 5(1)(e) gives the same right in NI.

Limits: no access if the record has a note, made at the patient's request, that they did not want access given on such an application. The holder must withhold anything not relevant to a claim arising from the death, and anything likely to cause serious harm or identifying third parties.
Access is free (1990 Act s 3(4)). The holder must respond within 21 days for records made in the last 40 days, otherwise 40 days. A medical examiner also has a right of access (s 3(1)(g)).

For living patients, the access provisions of the 1990 Act were repealed; access is under UK GDPR / DPA 2018. In Scotland, s 3(1)(ee) lets a person authorised under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 apply for an incapable living patient.

states.label: Patient alive (1990 Act access route not available)
Patient dead; person qualifies as PR or potential claimant
Access withheld in whole or part (patient's note; irrelevant, harmful or third-party information)

transitions.event: Application to holder of the record
conditions: Holder may ask for more information within 14 days to verify entitlement

transitions.event: Holder gives access within 21 or 40 days

deceasedPersonalDataProtected.note: UK data protection law protects only living individuals. DPA 2018 defines personal data as information about an identified or identifiable living individual, and UK GDPR recital 27 says the Regulation does not apply to deceased persons' data. Records of deceased patients are reached through the Access to Health Records Act 1990 (GB) and the 1993 NI Order instead. A common-law duty of confidence may survive death, but that is not verified here.

digitalAssetsFiduciaryStatute.name: None. No UK statute gives personal representatives, attorneys or deputies a right of access to a person's online accounts or digital assets. The Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 2025 (E&W and NI) only confirms that digital things can be personal property, so they can form part of an estate. In 2023 the Law Commission (Law Com No 412) noted that access to accounts on death and incapacity was outside its report and had been suggested as a separate project.

onlineToolsRecognisedInLaw.note: No UK statute recognises platform tools such as legacy contacts or inactive account managers. Law reform context only: Law Com No 412.
